scenes.title: Turn a customer message into a reliable picking list
points: Reserve stock or ask for clarification
scenes.narration: OrderClerk AI is a working counter desk for a small shop receiving written customer orders. A casual message can name products inconsistently, omit a quantity, or ask for stock that is no longer available. The aim is to help a clerk move from that message to a reliable picking list while keeping uncertain orders in review. This demonstration uses fictional customers and a synthetic catalogue priced in Zambian kwacha. It is a local prototype, not a connected WhatsApp or production shop system.

scenes.title: Local AI reads the customer note
scenes.narration: The clerk supplies a customer label, a stable message reference, and the original order message. The verified provider is Ollama running the pretrained Qwen two point five, three billion parameter model. The model proposes order lines and identifies unsupported products. Application code checks exact catalogue aliases and verifies explicit quantities next to their products in the original message. The quantity guard supports digits and English one through ten. Other or ambiguous phrasing is routed to review instead of receiving an invented number.

scenes.title: Two rice, one oil: K155, saved once
scenes.narration: The message asks for two bags of rice and one bottle of oil. The resulting order contains exactly those lines, using stored prices of fifty five kwacha per rice bag and forty five per oil bottle. The total is one hundred and fifty five kwacha. Stock falls from ten rice bags to eight, and from three oil bottles to two. The picking list can be downloaded as CSV. This screen also shows replay: submitting the same message reference returns the original order without reserving stock a second time.

scenes.title: A missing quantity becomes a question
scenes.narration: The next message says, I want rice. It contains no requested quantity, so the system asks how many bags are required and creates no order or reservation. This behavior was not assumed. An early model call guessed a quantity of one, which led to the source grounding guard. A model suggestion is accepted only after the application finds a valid explicit quantity for the product. This conservative boundary is useful because an invented number can become a real picking mistake.

scenes.title: A shortage stays at the desk
scenes.narration: Here the customer asks for five oil bottles. Only two remain after the first order, so the application reports the shortage and leaves stock unchanged. The same review path handles unsupported products. A normalized SQLite database separates customers, incoming messages, products, aliases, orders, line items, stock movements, reservations and events. Integer minor units avoid floating point money errors. A write transaction serializes stock decisions so two requests cannot both reserve the same last units.

scenes.title: Verified cases, clear limits, public code
points: Next: shop-owner feedback and broader language tests
scenes.narration: Nine automated tests cover the workflow, replay, concurrent stock protection, HTTP interface, source grounding and a database upgrade that preserves saved orders. Four real model scenarios passed: clear order, missing quantity, unsupported product and shortage. The repository contains the scripts and observed results. This small synthetic set is not a general accuracy benchmark, and no time savings or sales impact has been measured. OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation and documentation, and this narration is synthetic. A separately labeled offline parser is available; an optional OpenAI integration remains unverified. The next step is shop owner feedback and broader language testing.
